accuracy.evidence: Follows the KS2 statutory guidance for Years 3 and 4 (choosing nouns or pronouns appropriately for clarity and cohesion and to avoid repetition) and the topic evidence: rewriting 'Sam picked up Sam's bag', using reflexives correctly, and fixing 'Tom told Jack he was late'. Agreement in number and person (their for dogs, its for one tree, our for Raj and I) and the non-standard status of hisself and theirselves were checked against standard grammar references.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the real slips: replacing the first mention so no antecedent exists (step 1 rejects tapping the first Sam, mastery m5), number mismatch (its for dogs, his for the twins), ambiguous reference with two same-gender people, the non-standard hisself, ourself and theirselves, and using her/him where a reflexive is needed (Nia saw her in the mirror).

lab_distinct.evidence: Built around reference arrows: swapped pronouns draw a curve back to the name, the gap's antecedent is highlighted, the ambiguity step draws dashed lines from he/she/it to both possible people or things, and reflexive gaps loop back to the doer. Word chips are tapped in the sentence itself. Passed the 30% shingle gate against all labs.

lab_teaches.evidence: Steps follow the skill as children use it in writing: cut repetition, match the pronoun to its noun, notice when it could mean two people, use reflexives, then audit a passage. The arrows make 'points back to' visible before the message names the rule.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions with tempting wrong answers: change every Sam including the first (yes, every one), whether 'Tom told Jack he was late' tells us who was late (yes, Tom, the most common reading), and hisself versus himself, where hisself follows the his/her pattern and sounds right to many children.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating challenge items with tagged wrong options and specific messages: no name at all, repeated name, one-or-many mismatch, non-standard -self word, guessing a referent that could be either boy, and the unclear it. Every lab choice also has its own wrong-answer text (GAP.bad, AMB, REF.bad, MUD).

readability.evidence: Kid explanation is short sentences built from the lab's own examples and reads well under the family FK limit; the adult text is under the adult limit. Sentences on the canvas are four to ten words, and the terms pronoun, points back and -self word are shown in action before being named.

no_filler.evidence: The content gate found no filler and duplication with other lessons is under 12%. Every kid paragraph has a worked example, and the adult text covers only scope, lab actions, five named mistakes and one home check.

mobile.evidence: Walked on iPhone 13 and desktop: six steps, five tasks and the challenge all complete with Show me inside 6 seconds. Light-theme screenshots at 390 px show the word chips wrapping onto new lines with the arrows intact; the reflexive option text was shrunk on narrow screens after themselves/theirselves looked tight.

accessibility.evidence: axe found no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in either theme. Every canvas chip and option has an HTML button with a descriptive aria-label (for example 'Change Sam's, word 3' and 'Unclear word: she'), and the canvas aria-label reads out the current sentence and progress after each action.

sources: Department for Education (2013), English programmes of study: key stages 1 and 2, English Appendix 2 (Year 4: appropriate choice of pronoun or noun within and across sentences to aid cohesion and avoid repetition)
Department for Education (2013), Lower key stage 2 writing: vocabulary, grammar and punctuation
Cambridge Dictionary, English Grammar Today: reflexive pronouns (myself, himself, themselves) and the non-standard forms hisself and theirselves
Common Core State Standards for ELA, L.2.1c (use reflexive pronouns) and L.6.1d (recognise and correct vague pronouns)
